summary: Describes heuristics that help Telnet implementations of the Environment option work with others, by identifying which definitions of VAR and VALUE the other side is using.

eli5.summary: Two sides may use words differently. This memo gives clues for guessing which meaning the other side has in mind.

questions: what is the telnet environment option
why are var and value reversed in telnet
how to detect reversed var and value in telnet
subtitle: Heuristics for guessing whether the other side swapped VAR and VALUE in the Telnet Environment option.

tldr.problem: RFC 1408 defines VAR and VALUE the opposite way round from the BSD implementation it was meant to document, so implementations disagree.
tldr.mechanism: A client examines a SEND suboption, and a server examines an IS or INFO suboption, using a series of tests to decide whether the peer has the definitions reversed.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can interoperate with both conventions. When the tests are inconclusive, assume the peer is correct.

today: RFC 1571 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 1408. The unit metadata records no later RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: The VAR and VALUE Mix-up
sections.content:
RFC 1408, the specification of the Telnet Environment option, defines VAR and VALUE in the reverse of the BSD implementation. BSD was the reference implementation the RFC was supposed to document, and it is the base for many existing implementations, so implementations with conflicting definitions cannot interoperate.

This memo updates RFC 1408 with heuristics that help an implementation identify which definitions the other side uses.
sections.eli5: The written rules and the first working program disagree about two words. Both are in use, so programs need a way to tell which one they are talking to.

sections.title: What a Client Does
sections.content:
A SEND suboption should contain only VAR and USERVAR, never VALUE. If the client meets a VALUE while parsing it, the server has reversed the definitions, and the client reverses them from then on, both when parsing and when generating IS or INFO.

If both VALUE and VAR appear, the SEND is not well formed and the outcome is implementation dependent. If neither appears, the client assumes the server has the correct definitions.
sections.eli5: If the other side's list contains a word that should never be there, the client knows the meanings are swapped and swaps its own.

sections.title: What a Server Does
sections.content:
An IS or INFO suboption can legally be followed only by VAR or USERVAR. If it is followed by VAR, the client is correct. If followed by VALUE, the client is reversed.

When that is not decisive, the server applies further tests in order:

  • Two consecutive VARs or an empty VALUE mean the client is correct. Two consecutive VALUEs or an empty VAR mean it is reversed.
  • Count the VARs, USERVARs and VALUEs and compare the totals.
  • Check whether the VAR or the VALUE contents are well known variable names.
  • If everything fails, assume the client is correct.
sections.eli5: The server plays detective. It looks at the first clue, then at odd patterns, then at counting, then at whether the names look familiar. If it is still stuck, it trusts the other side.

sections.title: The Decision Rules at a Glance
sections.content:
The memo closes with two summaries. A client treats the server as correct if SEND has only VAR and USERVAR or has none of them, and as reversed if SEND contains VALUE.

A server treats the client as correct for IS/INFO followed by VAR, consecutive VARs, an empty VALUE, matching counts, well known VAR names, or anything else. It treats the client as reversed for the mirror-image cases.
sections.eli5: It is a short checklist: if you see the odd clue, the other side is swapped, otherwise assume everything is normal.

references.text: Borman, D., Editor, "Telnet Environment Option", RFC 1408, January 1993.
